title: How Mortgage-backed Securities Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and how subprime mortgage-backed securities helped trigger the 2008 economic downturn. They describe how individual mortgages are pooled, divided into shares, and sold to investors who collect payments; how demand for MBS pushed lenders toward subprime borrowers; how banks stopped carrying risk; how collateralized debt obligations repackaged MBS; and how foreclosures caused a housing market collapse, layoffs, and wider economic damage. They also discuss who is to blame, predatory lending, the lack of regulation on new financial instruments, and recommend related HowStuffWorks articles on the 2008 presidential and vice presidential candidates.

segments.title: Opening banter on the economic downturn
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about the US economy spiraling, mention investment banks failing and AIG being largely government-owned, and introduce mortgage-backed securities as the root cause.

segments.title: What a mortgage-backed security is
segments.summary: A mortgage-backed security is an investment based on a pool of mortgages divided into shares that pay dividends as homeowners make monthly payments. Investors can include banks, funds, and individuals, and some retirement or mutual fund holders may indirectly own shares of their own mortgage.

segments.title: How a mortgage becomes a security
segments.summary: A bank issues mortgages, sells batches to an investment bank, which pools several hundred mortgages into one security and sells shares to investors who collect dividends.

segments.title: Demand, subprime borrowers, and lending shift
segments.summary: Mortgage-backed securities became hot during a housing boom. Demand outstripped the supply of prime borrowers, so lenders turned to subprime borrowers, meaning people with weaker credit or income rather than a lower interest rate. Banks stopped holding the risk of default because they sold mortgages quickly.

segments.title: Collateralized debt obligations and risk
segments.summary: Mortgage-backed shares were repackaged into collateralized debt obligations, including ones made exclusively from subprime MBS. Higher interest rates on subprime loans meant higher dividends but greater risk, and the chain of buyers passed the securities along.

segments.title: Foreclosures, the domino effect, and blame
segments.summary: Once subprime borrowers defaulted and foreclosures spread around 2006, the securities tanked. Foreclosures lowered housing prices, unsold new homes led to construction layoffs and unemployment. The hosts discuss blame across lenders, brokers, investment banks, and borrowers, including predatory lending.

segments.title: Origins and lack of regulation of financial instruments
segments.summary: The hosts note that new financial instruments come from business schools and are modeled but not tested before release, and that no regulation requires testing them on a small scale first.

segments.title: Related articles and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh recommends HowStuffWorks articles on the 2008 presidential and vice presidential candidates, John McCain, Barack Obama, Sarah Palin, and Joe Biden, and invites listener feedback.
